newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-NORWEGIAN ROCKET BLAZES WINNING TRAIL.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-NORWEGIAN ROCKET BLAZES WINNING TRAIL.

text.p: After three days of patient waiting for a first gold medal, Norwegian fans were amply rewarded on Monday by the man they call the Norwegian Rocket.
They screamed in delight as Bjorn Daehlie blazed a trail on his way to a much-awaited triumph in Monday's 10-km classical style race at the Nordic skiing world championships.
Not only did the most succesful skier in cross-country history win. He crushed the opposition, leaving the silver and bronze medallists far behind.
Russian Alexei Prokurorov, who had defeated Daehlie in Friday's opening 30-km race, was 27.9 seconds slower while Finn Mika Myllylae was a further 4.5 seconds back.
"That man's from another planet," sighed a helpless Myllylae.
The win was particularly sweet for Daehlie, who had returned from the last world championships, in 1995 in Thunder Bay, Canada, with gold only in the relay.

"My last real win in a major event was in Lillehammer," he said, recalling his two titles in the 1994 Olympics. "I had made a gold medal in Trondheim my main goal a year ago. I worked hard for it and did all my planning and training with that in mind."

He started this season in style by scoring his 31st World Cup win last November in Kiruna, Sweden, beating the record of the man who has always been his example and inspiration, Swede Gunde Svan. Two more victories followed.
With six gold medals in world championships and five Olympic titles, the 29-year-old Daehlie was already ahead of Svan in the list of all-time greats before Monday's race. But he wanted more.
"Everybody was shouting for a Norwegian gold medal and I wanted to please them," he said. "My second place in the 30 km had showed me that I was in great shape and boosted my confidence."
With 20,000 fans lining the tracks, waving flags and ringing cowbells, and the rest of Norway watching on television, he just could not afford to fail.

"I started very strong and at one stage I thought that maybe I had started too fast," he said. "My legs were hurting and I was wondering if I would make it in the last uphill sections. But I heard all the people shout "Go for gold. Go for gold", and that gave me the strength to carry on."
Such is his status in Norway, no-one was surprised when after the 30 km, he went straight to King Harald to have a chat.
"He knows skiing very well and he asked me about my tactics," Daehlie said.

Because of his popularity, Daelhie advertises just about everything from ski wax to airlines. He appears almost every day in magazines, sometimes skiing, other times fishing salmon or enjoying a barbecue with friends.
What Norwegians like about him is that apart from being the number one personality in the number one sport, he is a straightforward, approachable character.
But, perhaps, he can be just a little bit too serious.
Before the start of the world championships, his team mates persuaded him to grow a moustache. But after the first race, he shaved it off.
"I'm faster without a moustache," he said at Monday's press conference. Everybody laughed. For Daehlie, that was a joke.

Some might say he lacks the charisma of genuine stars such as Alpine skiing showman Alberto Tomba but the Norwegians would not like him so much if he had a similarly tumultuous private life. They love him because he is just like them.
When they don't call him the Norwegian Rocket, they simply call him Bjorn.
